newsitem.title: IRAQ: Iraq urges U.N. to put arms inspector on trial.
newsitem.headline: Iraq urges U.N. to put arms inspector on trial.

text.p: An Iraqi official has urged the United Nations Security Council to put U.N. inspector Rolf Ekeus on trial for ordering the inspection last week of churches in Baghdad for hidden weapons.

"Abdul-al-Ghani Abdul-al-Ghafur (a senior ruling Baath party member and former culture and information minister)...demands the (U.N.) Security Council put Ekeus and the inspection team on trial ...because of the team's violation of places of worship," the government newspaper al-Jumhouriya said on Sunday.
Iraq said on Wednesday an arms team belonging to the U.N. Special Commission (UNSCOM) inspected a church and two convents in the outskirts of Baghdad, calling it a "flagrant aggression".

Deputy Chairman of UNSCOM Charles Duelfer said on Saturday: "We are convinced that there are prohibited things which Iraq is concealing, so we have no choice but to go after those locations where we think they may be concealed."

Rolf Ekeus, the chairman of UNSCOM, has complained to the U.N. Security Council that Baghdad prevented U.N. inspectors from entering three sites this month and had endangered U.N. helicopters and their crews assisting U.N. ground teams.

Late on Saturday, the United Nations Security Council responded to his complaints by unanimously warning Iraq it faced further sanctions if it did not allow U.N. arms inspectors to search sensitive sites.

Iraq's ruling Baath party newspaper al-Thawra said that Ekeus was implementing a U.S. anti-Iraq policy which was extending UNSCOM's mandate in Iraq in order to prolong the U.N. sanctions imposed for Iraq's 1990 invasion of Kuwait.

UNSCOM must certify Iraq has no weapons of mass destruction before the United Nations will lift curbs on its oil exports. The U.N. has allowed Baghdad since December to sell $2 billion worth of oil to buy urgently needed goods.
"The problem is that Ekeus himself is involved in serving American hostile policy against Iraq," Thawra said in a front-page editorial.
